metadata.note: The Boyne City, Gaylord and Alpena Railroad ('the White Road') and its predecessor the Boyne City and South Eastern, drawn from the research report research/branches/boyne_city_gaylord_and_alpena_railroad.txt (2026-11-02) on 2026-11-02. Before this layer the map drew nothing of this road. Only the report's drawable spans are drawn. Three companies, three colours (Rule 4): Boyne City and South Eastern 1901-1905, Boyne City, Gaylord and Alpena 1905-1926, and the Boyne City Railroad's 1971-1973 tourist excursions; the BC&SE / BCG&A split at the 1905 purchase shares identical geometry, as does the 1971-73 Boyne City Railroad feature. The Michigan Central offered to buy the road in 1930-32 but never did, so there is no NYC-coloured successor.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: OPEN ENDS - every BCG&A end year (Boyne City - Boyne Falls, Boyne Falls - Gaylord, Gaylord - Atlanta, Atlanta - Alpena) is 1926, the last CONFIRMED passenger year (Fowler's 'b' = 1926 Official Guide), not a known end; no source dates the last passenger train on any piece. Trains ran to 1 Dec 1931 (Atlanta - Alpena suspended by 10 Mar 1931 after flooding); a dated 1927-31 newspaper item or Official Guide/Michigan Guide entry showing the motor car carrying passengers would extend these. Whether passengers rode Boyne City - Boyne Falls 1932-1935 or later is unknown (freight-only by the Feb 1952 Guide). OPEN START - the BC&SE is drawn from 1901 (first confirmed year); built 1893 (michiganrailroads) vs organised 1897 (PNR 1960). BCG&A incorporation 1905 (ICC) vs 1903 (PNR 1960). Alpena completion 15 Aug vs 20 Dec 1918. Tourist era 1970/1971 start and 1973/1975 end in conflict. Whether the USRA operated the road in 1918 is not established. The Boyne Falls station site and the BCG&A's Alpena terminal approach (last ~1.5 mi) are not located. All headways and speeds are estimates. Station-level data (Rule 8) has not been started for this railroad.
metadata.branches_deliberately_omitted: Boyne Valley Railroad tourist excursions 1976-77 (claimed, no dated report - report block [7], drawable NONE); Thumb Lake Branch [8], BC&SE camp branches incl. White's Jct - Camp No. 2 and Maple Slope - White Headquarters Camp [9], Southend Branch [10] and the Dobbins/Rust logging spurs [11] (logging, no passenger evidence, Rule 1); the proposed Alpena - Rockport and cement shale-bed extensions [12] (never built); the BC&SE's 1893-1900 years and the BCG&A's 1914-1918 Gaylord - Atlanta years (built, but no passenger year confirmed).
metadata.freight_only_excluded: Boyne City Railroad, Boyne City - Boyne Falls 1935-1970 (freight, LCL and express only; Feb 1952 Official Guide index daggers Boyne City 'for freight only') [13]; Boyne Valley Railroad 1976-78 freight if any; the main line 1932-1935 (track standing, out of use).
metadata.horsecar_audit: None needed: steam from the outset (BC&SE 1902 locomotive roster), gasoline motor cars from 1910. Nothing trimmed (Rule 5).

segments.note: The W. H. White lumber company's Boyne City and South Eastern, built 1893 (michiganrailroads; a 1960 Petoskey News-Review article says 'organized in 1897' - conflict recorded). Drawn from 1901 [OPEN START]: 1901 is the earliest CONFIRMED passenger year (Fowler's '1901t' company-timetable tags at Thumb Lake Junction and White's Junction); 1893-1900 passenger service is unproven, not disproven. The Michigan Commissioner of Railroads' 1902 report (quoted by michiganrailroads) records a heated passenger car, conductors and 12 stations. 1905 is a corporate end only: the Boyne City, Gaylord and Alpena bought the line in 1905 (ICC valuation) and service continued under it. Steam from the outset; no animal traction (Rule 5). The 1902 'main line' of 19.6 mi ran on east of Boyne Falls as logging track and is not drawn. Headway is an estimate and is NOT sourced.

segments.note: The BCG&A bought the Boyne City and South Eastern in 1905 (ICC valuation; a 1960 Petoskey News-Review article says 1903 - conflict recorded) and ran this stub as the west end of its line; drawn from 1905 to continue the BC&SE seamlessly (first year proven under the BCG&A name is 1906). Receivership (Michigan Trust Co.) Nov 1913 - c.1917/18 operated the same company's trains, so no split. Fowler lists Doyle's Siding and Cushman in the 1909 Woods Michigan Guide and Boyne City and Boyne Falls in the 1926 Official Guide. In Feb-Apr 1925 the dispatcher's order book shows trains No. 1/2, a Boyne City - Boyne Falls shuttle, every weekday plus through trains No. 17/18 to Alpena; the headway (about two trains each way a day) is an estimate from that order book, which does not itself say the trains carried passengers. This end year is the last CONFIRMED passenger year (Fowler's 'b' letter = the 1926 Official Guide; his legend defines no later letter for this road), NOT a known end. Trains ran on this section into 1931 and a gasoline motor car described elsewhere as a passenger/mail car was 'practically all the company has had on the line ... for about four years' (Detroit Free Press 29 Nov 1931), but no source dated after 1926 says passengers were carried. Do not extend without evidence. On this stub the open question runs to 1935: whether the BCG&A kept a passenger car here after through trains east of Boyne Falls stopped (Dec 1931 / 1932) is not established. From 1935 the Boyne City Railroad carried freight, LCL and express only, and the Feb 1952 Official Guide daggers Boyne City 'for freight only' - not drawn (Rule 1).
sources: Segment-level: 1905 start = BCG&A purchase (ICC valuation); 1909 stations = Fowler 1909WG; 1926 end = Fowler 'b' (1926 Official Guide) at Boyne City and Boyne Falls, [OPEN]; 1925 trains = dispatcher's order book. Headway is an estimate. (as checked by the research report research/branches/boyne_city_gaylord_and_alpena_railroad.txt (2026-11-02))

No straight-line leg: entirely on the OHM way OHM labels 'Boyne City Southeastern Railroad / W.H. White Lumber Company 1893-1905' (OHM's dating, which conflicts with the report: the line reached Gaylord in 1905 under the BCG&A; the geometry is used, not the dates). Starts at the line's closest approach to Boyne Falls village (see the Boyne City - Boyne Falls feature: about 0.9 mi less than Fowler's MP 7.2 is drawn west of here, which is why this feature measures 0.9 mi over Fowler) and ends at the Michigan Central crossing at Gaylord. Check of the OHM line against Fowler's mileposts, measured along the drawn line from its Boyne City end: the GR&I overhead crossing at North Elmira falls at 13.23 mi (Fowler 13.2), the Michigan Central crossing at Gaylord at 23.22 mi (Fowler 23.2), Sparr 29.0 (28.8), Rust 63.0 (62.7), Spratt 74.0 (74.4), Herron 79.1 (80.3), McHarg 81.5 (81.4). segments.note: The BCG&A's extension to the Michigan Central's Mackinaw Division at Gaylord (track reached Gaylord 25 Nov 1905 per Wikipedia; 'between 1905 and 1907' per the ICC valuation). Drawn from 1906, the first CONFIRMED passenger year: the Michigan Central's Detroit passenger agent announced the line's completion to Gaylord and 'Two BCG&A trains run west daily from here' (Detroit Free Press 1 July 1906, quoted on michiganrailroads' Gaylord page). Fowler lists Project and Hamilton in the 1909 Woods guide; first motor-car trip Boyne City - Gaylord and return 1910. The 1925 order book shows one through round trip (No. 17/18) a weekday - the headway is an estimate from it. This end year is the last CONFIRMED passenger year (Fowler's 'b' letter = the 1926 Official Guide; his legend defines no later letter for this road), NOT a known end. Trains ran on this section into 1931 and a gasoline motor car described elsewhere as a passenger/mail car was 'practically all the company has had on the line ... for about four years' (Detroit Free Press 29 Nov 1931), but no source dated after 1926 says passengers were carried. Do not extend without evidence. The line was unused from 1932 (Detroit Free Press 9 Oct 1949) and pulled up in 1935.

properties.geometry_quality: 37.7 mi drawn Atlanta - BCG&A Junction against 39.1 mi documented Atlanta - Alpena (Fowler MPs 52.9-92.0; ICC main line 91.52 mi in all). No straight-line leg, but two caveats: (1) the last 8.4 mi, McHarg - BCG&A Junction, is OHM way 198826096 (dated 20 Dec 1918), which is nearly straight - 21 vertices, at most 185 m off its own chord - so it may be the OHM mapper's generalisation of the grade rather than a faithful trace; (2) the line stops where that OHM way ends, at the Detroit and Mackinac main line about 2.8 km north of Alpena's centre (BCG&A Junction). The last ~1.5 mi into the BCG&A's Alpena terminal (about 1 mi from the city centre, on D&M terminal facilities rented from 1918) is NOT drawn, because its route is not sourced. Rust, Spratt, Herron and McHarg each lie within 0.1 km of the line; the Fletcher Floodwaters section (track still under the reservoir) is drawn on its original alignment. One alignment known.

segments.note: Completed to Alpena in 1918 - date in conflict: 15 Aug 1918 ('most histories', michiganrailroads) vs 20 Dec 1918 (Wikipedia) vs '1919' (1920 trial report). The eastern 24 mi were built west from Alpena c.1912-14 with local money; no evidence that section carried passengers before the 1918 junction. Drawn from 1919, the first CONFIRMED passenger year (Fowler's 'a' at Dobbins, Rust, Spratt, Stinson, Herron and McHarg). For the Kerston - Alpena tip only 1926 is confirmed by Fowler; drawing it from 1919 follows the 1918 completion and the 1919 listings to McHarg. Whether the USRA operated the road after the Director of Railroads' May 1918 announcement is not established. By 10 Mar 1931 trucks had replaced trains Alpena - Atlanta for mail and express after Alpena Power Co.'s dam flooded the track (Fletcher Floodwaters); trains formally ceased 1 Dec 1931. Headway (one through round trip a weekday in 1925) is an estimate from the dispatcher's order book. This end year is the last CONFIRMED passenger year (Fowler's 'b' letter = the 1926 Official Guide; his legend defines no later letter for this road), NOT a known end. Trains ran on this section into 1931 and a gasoline motor car described elsewhere as a passenger/mail car was 'practically all the company has had on the line ... for about four years' (Detroit Free Press 29 Nov 1931), but no source dated after 1926 says passengers were carried. Do not extend without evidence.
sources: Segment-level: 1918 completion conflict = michiganrailroads timetable page vs Wikipedia; 1919 start = Fowler 'a' (to McHarg); Alpena itself only Fowler 'b'; 1926 end = Fowler 'b', [OPEN]; 1931 = SJH 1931-03-10 and DFP 1931-11-29. Headway is an estimate. (as checked by the research report research/branches/boyne_city_gaylord_and_alpena_railroad.txt (2026-11-02))

segments.note: Summer tourist excursions after freight ended in 1970: the British steam locomotive 'Flying Duchess' with British Rail Mk 1 coaches, and a GE 44-ton diesel with open observation cars; three round trips daily in summer, about 25,000 riders a year (AP 1976, Boyne Falls History). Start 1971: the Flying Duchess 'began its operations at the BCRR on July 24, 1971' (Wikipedia); a michiganrailroads postcard caption says 1970 - conflict recorded. End 1973 per the AP (engineer Fineout: 'The energy crisis forced the line to close in 1973'), Boyne Falls History and Wikipedia; the Detroit Free Press (2 May 1976) says the line stopped in Oct 1975 'after just two summers' - conflict recorded, drawn to the earlier reading. The Boyne Valley Railroad's claimed 1976-77 excursions are not drawn (no dated report). Headway is an estimate from 'three round trips daily'. The 1935-1970 freight-only years are not drawn (Rule 1).
